name: Custom chin implant (silicone/Medpor)

lead: A chin implant is a shaped piece of silicone or porous polyethylene (Medpor) placed over the chin bone to push a recessed chin forward. It gives a stronger, more balanced side profile, and can also add height or width.

The implant sits on the front of the jawbone and adds bulk through a cut under the chin or inside the lower lip. Silicone is smooth and removable; porous polyethylene allows tissue ingrowth. Custom implants are designed from a CT scan of the individual's jaw. It is a long-established cosmetic operation, often done alongside nose surgery, and outcomes are documented mainly in surgical case series.

paras: People usually see a surgeon for a consultation and imaging, then have a short operation under anaesthetic. It is often chosen as a less invasive alternative to a sliding genioplasty, and is frequently combined with rhinoplasty. Swelling settles over weeks and the final profile is visible once healed. Forum users compare stock implants with custom designs and discuss whether an implant is enough for a very recessed chin.

Reported risks include swelling, hematoma, infection, implant displacement, bone changes under the implant and nerve numbness. Complication rates depend on technique and surgeon experience. Implants can shift or be removed later, and porous polyethylene is harder to remove than silicone. It is an Rx surgical procedure performed by licensed surgeons.

angle.text: A chin implant adds projection, and sometimes height or width, to a recessed chin by placing material over the chin bone. The stronger, more balanced profile is visible once healed. Silicone, porous polyethylene and patient-specific designs are used, with outcomes documented in surgical case series.

lead: A custom or alloplastic chin implant is a shaped piece of synthetic material, most often silicone or porous high-density polyethylene (sold as Medpor), placed on the front of the lower jaw to bring a recessed chin forward. For people who feel their profile is dominated by a small chin, it changes the lower third of the face from the side: a more projected chin lengthens the visual line from lip to neck and balances the nose and forehead. [1][2]

The operation is among the older procedures in facial plastic surgery and is frequently performed together with rhinoplasty or a facelift. Surgeons describe it as an adjunct that rebalances the profile rather than a stand-alone change in most cases, and review articles describe long-running debate over whether implant placement or osseous (bone-cutting) genioplasty is the better operation for a given patient. [3][2][4]

In looksmaxxing communities the implant is discussed as a lower-cost, less invasive and potentially reversible alternative to a sliding genioplasty, and the word 'custom' refers to a design made from the individual's CT scan, usually in PEEK, titanium or Medpor rather than an off-the-shelf silicone shape. Published research is mostly narrative reviews, retrospective series and a few small registered trials, and it includes comparisons of implants with genioplasty and of silicone with porous polyethylene. [5][6][7][4][4]

paras: The chin (mentum) is the forward part of the mandible. In a person whose chin sits behind the line of the lips and nose, the profile can look receded, and clinicians use the term microgenia for a small chin. An implant is a prefabricated or individually made solid shape that lies on the bone at the lower border of the jaw and is held in a pocket beneath the periosteum and soft tissue, or fixed to bone with screws. [2][4]

Surgeons place it through a cut beneath the chin or through the inside of the lower lip. Reported benefits include a shorter operation than a bone-moving procedure, no cut through the jawbone, and, for some materials, the option of removal. [2]

Oral and maxillofacial surgeons, otolaryngologists and plastic surgeons all perform chin augmentation, and a small chin that comes with a significant overbite may instead be treated with mandibular advancement (orthognathic) surgery, which corrects the bite along with the chin. [2]

Silicone is soft and flexible, and does not bond to surrounding tissue, so the pocket has to be made precisely. Because it is smooth, it can be removed easily. Encyclopedic summaries note that it can shift and that it may press on the underlying bone and cause resorption. [2][1]

Medpor is firm, porous and slightly flexible. Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors it and supports a blood supply, and the same ingrowth makes later removal harder. [2] On looksmax.org, users who prefer other materials mention the vascular ingrowth as a reason to avoid it, while others rank PEEK and Medpor as good all-round materials. [8][9]

Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) is soft yet strong and porous, and is screwed to bone with titanium. Acellular dermis (AlloDerm) is used to cover implants. Supramid and Mersiline have also been described, and rib or pelvic bone grafts have been used and are linked in summaries to a higher infection rate. [2]

Custom implants are designed from a CT scan and fabricated to the person's jaw, usually in PEEK, titanium or porous polyethylene, sometimes with the surgeon's cutting guides. Registered trials have examined the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants for chin deficiency and of patient-specific implants in genioplasty. [6][7] Forum members describe paying more for scan-based designs and share before-and-after photos of them. [10][11]

A sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped segment from the lower jaw and moves it forward, holding it with a titanium plate or fine wires, so that the chin's own bone is repositioned rather than adding material. [2] A bone-based correction usually produces a more dramatic change than a prosthetic implant, according to encyclopedic summaries. [1][2]

In 1990, Guyuron and Raszewski compared 34 patients who had osteoplastic genioplasty with 42 who had implants, using questionnaires. Both groups reported high satisfaction, slightly higher after osteotomy; morbidity was the same, soft-tissue response was more predictable with osteoplastic genioplasty, and it improved the cervicomental angle more. The authors recommended osteoplastic genioplasty broadly while allowing that an implant could suit older patients with mild microgenia. [4]

A 2011 review of complications in chin augmentation states that the debate over implant versus osseous genioplasty continues and that surgeons should use the techniques that work best in their own hands. [3] A 2013 review in Seminars in Plastic Surgery covers both approaches, together with chin movement combined with orthognathic surgery, and stresses assessment of skeletal, soft-tissue and dental balance. [4] On looksmax.org, users weigh the two options by cost, reversibility and whether an implant could stand in while waiting for a bone-moving operation.

The immediate result of an implant is a measurable increase in chin projection, and surgical authors describe chin augmentation as a rewarding cosmetic operation, especially as an adjunct to nose and facelift surgery. [3] Studies of facial cosmetic surgery more broadly have used observer ratings to examine perceived attractiveness and personality traits; they are not specific to chin implants. [12][13]

Satisfaction in the comparison above was high with implants and with osteotomy. [4] Registered trials (NCT04817930, NCT03577210, NCT03456869) are examining patient-specific implants for accuracy and soft-tissue outcomes after one year. [5][6][7]

Swelling, bruising, a haematoma, and temporary lower-lip numbness or weakness are common and usually minor. Less common are infection, implant displacement, bone changes and nerve damage, and surgeon experience is described as reducing these. [3][2]

Silicone implants can erode the mandible beneath them. A 1996 retrospective series of six patients with Silastic implants linked pre-operative labial incompetence and mentalis muscle hyperactivity with progressive bone erosion, some of it severe; the authors suggested follow-up examinations and radiographs for such patients because erosion can be symptom-free for a long time. [4] On looksmax.org members debate whether silicone erodes bone and how often, with some citing the literature and others reporting no problems. [8][14]

subs.h: Silicone versus Medpor in the literature
paras: A 2018 systematic review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery covered mandible, malar and chin implants: nine studies with 626 Medpor patients and five with 365 silicone patients. Silicone showed more infections and displacements, Medpor more prominence problems, and extrusion was low for both; chin and mandibular implants had the fewest problems. The authors noted that follow-up is short, with means of 36.6 months for Medpor and 24 months for silicone, and that follow-up has not improved in 20 years. [4]

Forum threads ask whether a chin implant is 'enough' on its own, whether it suits a recessed chin with a short face, and request ratings of before-and-after photos. [10] Others ask about swelling timelines after Medpor, silicone and PEEK implants, and how long until the final shape shows. [15]

Some members ask about a vertical-lengthening implant versus a vertical genioplasty for a taller chin.  Others discuss fat grafting as a softer alternative, and the surgical literature describes autologous fat grafting to the chin as an adjunct in facial rejuvenation. [16] Non-surgical options include hyaluronic acid and calcium hydroxyapatite fillers, which are temporary; permanent liquid silicone injection has fallen out of favour because of migration and inflammation reports. [2]

Published surgical literature consists mainly of narrative reviews and case series. [3][17][4] A 1981 clinical analysis of alloplastic implants in The Laryngoscope is an early series; the 1990 questionnaire comparison and the 1996 case series on bone resorption are retrospective. [17][4][4] The 2018 systematic review pooled Medpor and silicone studies for complications. [4]

A registered trial (NCT04817930, completed, 20 participants) compared a patient-specific alloplastic chin implant with computer-guided genioplasty, assessing soft-tissue results after one year. [5] Other registered trials have examined the accuracy of patient-specific PEEK implants and of patient-specific implants in genioplasty. [6][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chin implants are discussed in threads comparing them with sliding genioplasty and filler, in custom-implant result posts, in material comparisons (silicone, Medpor, PEEK, titanium) and in questions about insurance and removal. [8][9]
